oralTraditions.claim: Among the Fula of western Burkina Faso, the Diallo and the Diakité form one of the two pairs that make up the mythical core of Fula identity. One narrative says that, during a flight after a defeat, a Diallo revives a fainting Diakité by making him eat part of his own flesh, and that the two clans sealed an alliance on that occasion.
oralTraditions.griot: Informateurs peuls de l'ouest du Burkina Faso, non nommés dans l'article
oralTraditions.transcription: Narrative summarised by the author, not transcribed word for word: Diallo, Youssouf, « Identités et relations de plaisanterie chez les Peuls de l'ouest du Burkina Faso », Cahiers d'études africaines, no. 184, 2006, pp. 779-794.

writtenChronicles.claim: The earliest written attestation of the name found in the sources consulted dates from 1734. Bluett records that the countrymen of Ayuba Suleiman Diallo "designate themselves by the names of their ancestors" and trace them back several degrees, "although they also have family names to distinguish their particular families"; for the same man he gives the patronymic chain HYUBA, BOON SALUMENA, BOON HIBRAHEMA — Ayuba son of Suleiman son of Ibrahim — and then, separately, "The Surname of his Family is Jallo". The name is therefore already, in 1734, a hereditary family name held to be distinct from the filiation stated degree by degree.

Bluett places the family at Boonda, in Bundu, on the upper Senegal, and reports that Ayuba's grandfather, Ibrahim, had founded the town there some fifty years earlier under the reign of Bubaker, king of Futa, combining the eminent ownership of the place with the office of high priest (alpha); he had established there that no one taking refuge in it could be reduced to slavery. Bluett's geography is that of the maps of his time and contradicts itself: the clan claim of Fouta-Djalon and this Bundu lineage are not related to each other by any source consulted.

The Fula group of western Burkina Faso is made up of four main clans, Diallo, Diakité, Sidibé and Sangaré. The Diallo and the Diakité form one of the two pairs of the mythical core of Fula identity, in a relation of equivalence, and the Diallo are also held to be counterparts of the Diko, with whom they have a joking relationship.

Almost all the Fulbe of Guinea bear one of four family names: Diallo, also written Jalloh, Barry, Balde, also written Bah, and Sow. The name Diallo covers about one tenth of the Guinean population, without being more widespread than the other three.

linguisticReconstructions.claim: The name belongs to the four clans by which the Fulɓe identify themselves — Diallo, Bâ, Barry and Sow — whose fourfold division structures clan identification in Fouta.

A dictionary of family names lists Diallo among the clan names of the Fula and declares its etymology unexplained. It notes that the name is also found among other peoples, the Bambara for example, and gives Jalloh, mainly in Sierra Leone, and Jallow, mainly in the Gambia, as variants of the same name.

The dictionary of Bambara clan names has no entry for Jalo, but it cites this name as a joking partner of the Bagayogo, Dansoko and Janka clans, and as an equivalent of Dikko, a Fula, Toucouleur and Dogon entry whose equivalence is marked with a doubt, and of Suntura, a Fula entry.

sources.title: Relevé de couverture anthroponymique EthniAfrica
sources.notes: This name is on our list of names to document: it was selected as a name to be documented, but no dedicated source has yet been consulted. The fiche therefore exists to point to the name, not for what it asserts about it. Further checks will draw on electoral registers, national statistical institutes and onomastic studies of the country concerned.

sources.title: Some Memoirs of the Life of Job, the Son of Solomon, the High Priest of Boonda in Africa
sources.notes: Bluett, Thomas, London, 1734. Primary document: the account dictated by Ayuba Suleiman Diallo to Bluett during his captivity, printed in his lifetime. It is the earliest known written attestation of the name, and it is explicit about the system: "The Surname of his Family is Jallo", set beside the patronymic chain "HYUBA, BOON SALUMENA, BOON HIBRAHEMA". The URL is the excerpted edition of the National Humanities Center (2009), the only version whose text could be read in full here; the complete text is at Documenting the American South (docsouth.unc.edu/neh/bluett/menu.html), whose server refused the connection at the time of consultation. Sections I and III verified word for word. A colonial source, to be read as such: Bluett writes in English, as an Anglican abolitionist, about a man whom he helped to free, and the spelling "Jallo" is his own.

sources.title: Autoportrait du Mali — Les Obstacles à la Paix
sources.notes: Action-research report of the Institut malien de recherche action pour la paix with Interpeace, in partnership with the United Nations, March 2015. Its chapter on sociocultural diversity gives, for each major group in Mali, a few family names followed by "etc.": the list is illustrative, with no method of compilation or source indicated. It attests that a name is borne within a group, not where it comes from.

sources.title: Études synchroniques des ethnies et des langues au Mali
sources.notes: Salif Sy, ARLAP research notebook (Hypotheses.org), 18 February 2015. Post by a doctoral student in African languages, without peer review, which lists Diallo, Diakité, Sidibé and Sangaré among the names identified as Fula in Mali. Cited to attest the name in this group and in this country, not for its origin.

sources.title: Identités et relations de plaisanterie chez les Peuls de l'ouest du Burkina Faso
sources.notes: Youssouf Diallo, Cahiers d'études africaines, vol. 46, no. 184, 2006, pp. 779-794 (DOI 10.4000/etudesafricaines.15399). Peer-reviewed journal; the author was then affiliated with the Max-Planck-Institut für ethnologische Forschung. The fieldwork concerns the Fula of western Burkina Faso, which attests the names in that country. The article says that the Fula group is made up of four main clans (Diallo, Diakité, Sidibé, Sangaré), that the pairs Diallo/Diakité and Sidibé/Sangaré, the mythical core of Fula identity, are in a relation of equivalence, and that Diallo/Diko, Diakité/Ba and Sidibé/Sangaré are counterparts and as such have joking relationships (dendiraagu). It also reports an alliance narrative between a Diallo and a Diakité.

sources.title: Pouvoir, places et filiation : les senankuya au Mali
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, Cahiers de praxématique, no. 38, 2002, pp. 175-197. Fieldwork in Mali. It states what the pact requires: the relationship holds in perpetuity for all the descendants of the two lineages, marriage between them is prohibited — applied in varying ways today, she specifies — and mutual aid is owed without reservation. Cited for the obligation itself; it does not name the pair of this fiche, which is carried by the entries cited alongside it.

sources.title: Pactes, alliances et plaisanteries. Pratiques locales, discours global
sources.notes: Canut, Cécile, and Smith, Étienne, Cahiers d'études africaines, no. 184, 2006, p. 687 ff. Cited for the caution it carries: the idea that joking kinship would ease conflicts is treated there as a hypothesis inherited from Radcliffe-Brown and taken up by conflict resolution studies, therefore as a discourse to be analysed and not as a measured effect. The first page is verified, the last page is not.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Onomastic annex of the Bamadaba, the electronic Bambara-French dictionary supplementing the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA); the annex of clan names is identified as such by Vydrin, « Vers une lexicographie mandingue sur la base de grands corpus annotés », Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. 375 entries in MDF format, consulted in the complete file. Jalo has no entry of its own there: the name is cited as a joking partner (marker \sn, read senankun) by the entries Bagayogo, Dansoko and Janka, and as an equivalent (marker \eq) under the entries Dikko, with a question mark and a distribution marked Fula, Toucouleur and Dogon, and Suntura, marked Fula. The \sn links are not systematically reciprocal from one entry to another: each pair is therefore cited according to the entry that carries it.

sources.title: Dictionary of American Family Names, 2e édition — entrées Diallo, Jalloh et Jallow
sources.notes: Patrick Hanks (ed.), Dictionary of American Family Names, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press, 2022; consulted through the Geneanet page that reproduces the entries with their source statement. Reference work: Diallo is given there as the name of the Diallo clan of the Fula, of unexplained etymology, also borne among other peoples such as the Bambara; Jalloh and Jallow are West African variants of Diallo.

sources.title: Does Dominique Strauss-Kahn's accuser, Nafissatou Diallo, have the most common surname in Guinea?
sources.notes: Maura Kelly, Slate, 27 July 2011. Press article drawing on several cited specialists (United States Census Bureau, Family Names Research Project, Yale, American Name Society). It says that almost all the Fulbe bear one of four names — Diallo (also written Jalloh), Barry, Balde (also written Bah) and Sow — that Diallo covers about 10% of the Guinean population, and that nearly two in five Guineans are Fulbe.

sources.title: Diallo — origine, signification et répartition du nom
sources.notes: Aggregator site of surname statistics, with no verifiable independent editorial review; data from 2014, consulted in an archived copy from 2023. It counts about 3.76 million bearers: Guinea 1,964,007, Senegal 668,185, Mali 536,347, Burkina Faso 359,891, Mauritania 83,187, Côte d'Ivoire 42,431, Guinea-Bissau 14,260, the Gambia 4,558, Liberia 1,187, and figures outside Africa, including France (19,312), which are not carried into the attestations. gaps.reason: Bluett gives Ayuba's lineage a hereditary religious office — his grandfather and then his father were alpha, high priest of Boonda, and he himself assisted his father — but it attaches to a specific family of Bundu, not to the name: the source says nothing of a function borne by the Jallo as such. The specialist castes of Futa also bear other names.

The onomastic reference works consulted leave the etymology of Diallo unexplained: no established Pulaar root supports it, and Bluett, who nonetheless gives the 1734 form, proposes none. The proposed connections — to a jallo said to mean "command", or to Mandinka diala for nobility — are corroborated by no primary linguistic source and resemble folk etymologies born of Fula-Mandinka contact. The absence of an established etymology is here the result of the research, not a shortcoming of it. The transcriptions Jallo, Jalloh, Jallow and Djaló designate the same name and are therefore not homonyms.
